title: Global HIV Funding Falls 18 Percent, Threatening Decades of Progress
excerpt: UNAIDS warns of epidemic resurgence as international support drops to its lowest level in nearly two decades, with prevention services in sub-Saharan Africa hit hardest.
body:
• Global HIV funding fell 18 percent to $7.3 billion in 2025, the lowest level in nearly two decades, according to a UNAIDS report released at the International AIDS Conference in Brazil.
  • The United States previously accounted for 75 percent of international HIV funding before President Trump's return to the White House triggered temporary halts and ongoing cuts.
  • Across 62 countries, 38 percent fewer people received pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in 2025 compared to the previous year, a decline of 1.2 million people.
  • Modeling studies project that current funding cuts could result in 10 million additional HIV infections and 3 million additional deaths over five years.

An Epidemic at Risk of Reversal

The world risks a resurgence of the HIV epidemic after global funding fell by nearly a fifth last year, UNAIDS warned in a 60-page report released at the start of the International AIDS Conference in Brazil.

Funding dropped 18 percent to $7.3 billion in 2025, the lowest level in almost two decades. The decline threatens to reverse progress that has driven new HIV infections and AIDS-related deaths to their lowest level in more than 30 years.

"We are undergoing perhaps the most serious disruption of HIV services since the HIV response started. We can't sit here thinking that the impact isn't so dramatic."

— Winnie Byanyima, Executive Director, UNAIDS

US Funding Cuts Drive the Crisis

Washington had accounted for 75 percent of international HIV funding through PEPFAR, the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief. When President Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, he ordered a temporary halt to all HIV-related funding. While life-saving treatment work was restored days later, most prevention efforts were curtailed and have not recovered.

The Clinton Health Access Initiative found that HIV services have not recovered a year into the funding crisis. US funding agreements with 11 countries project declines of 42 to 97 percent by 2030. The main US-funded logistics operation covering drug distribution is winding down, with most countries losing that support by September 2026.

Prevention Services Collapse

The damage is concentrated in prevention. Across 62 countries, 38 percent fewer people received pre-exposure prophylaxis in 2025 compared to the previous year — a drop of 1.2 million people, from 3.3 million to 2.1 million. Cameroon, Nigeria, and Zambia saw more than a 50 percent decline in PrEP access. Funding for condoms fell by more than 90 percent in some countries.

The irony is brutal: the cuts come just as a breakthrough prevention drug, lenacapavir, has demonstrated near-total effectiveness in clinical trials. The twice-yearly injection could transform prevention, but the funding infrastructure needed to deploy it is collapsing.

Modeling the Catastrophe

Multiple modeling studies project devastating consequences. A consensus of nine statistical models reviewed by Duke University researchers predicts 10 million additional HIV infections and 3 million additional deaths over five years if current cuts continue. Some 1.2 million people caught HIV last year.

Domestic spending increases have partially offset international cuts, but not all governments can step in. Sub-Saharan Africa, which accounts for about half of new global infections, has seen some of the biggest declines in prevention spending. The global goal to end AIDS by 2030 is off track.
